name: Singleton
intent: Guarantee a class has exactly one instance and give everyone a single way to reach it.
scenario: An app has shared settings (theme, language). The header and footer must always see the same AppConfig.
problem: Some things should exist once: app settings, a connection pool, a logger. If every component creates its own copy with new, each copy holds different data. The header sets the theme to dark, the footer asks a different object and sees nothing.
solution: Make the constructor unavailable to outsiders and expose one access point, usually getInstance(). The first call creates the object. Every later call returns that same object.
pain: Header and Footer each create their own AppConfig
A setting saved in one copy is invisible in the other
Nothing stops a third or fourth copy from appearing
Expensive setup (files, connections) is repeated per copy
benefits: Everyone shares one AppConfig, so settings always agree
The constructor refuses outside callers, so duplicates cannot appear
The instance is created once, on first use
There is one obvious place to get it: getInstance()
whenToUse: Exactly one shared object is a real rule of the domain: configuration, a hardware handle, a connection pool
Creation is expensive and you want to do it lazily and once
You need a controlled single access point
whenNotToUse: You only want convenient global access. Pass the object in as a parameter instead
You need to test code in isolation: global state leaks between tests
The "one instance" rule may change later, for example one per tenant or per user
pitfalls: Hidden dependency: code that calls getInstance() looks independent but is not
Thread safety: two threads can create two instances unless creation is guarded (C# Lazy<T> handles this)
Hard to test and to replace with a fake
Often used as a polite global variable; prefer dependency injection when you can

roles.label: Singleton
roles.description: Holds the one instance, hides its constructor, exposes getInstance().

roles.label: Client
roles.description: Any code that needs the shared object and asks getInstance() for it.

quiz.question: An app creates its AppConfig with new in the header and again in the footer. The header sets the theme to dark, but the footer still renders the default theme. What is the best fix?
options: Call setTheme in the footer too, so both copies are kept in step by hand
Hide the constructor and let both components get the single shared instance from one access point
Copy the theme from the header into the footer's own AppConfig when the page loads
Create the AppConfig earlier in the program so the footer is the one that has the value
quiz.explanation: The root cause is two separate objects. One private constructor and one access point such as getInstance() means there is only one object to disagree with. Copying values or calling setters twice keeps two objects that can drift again.

quiz.question: A getInstance() method does: if the instance is empty, build a ConnectionPool of 20 connections, then store it. At startup two requests call it at the same moment, with no lock. What can happen?
options: Both threads see an empty instance and each build a pool, so up to 40 connections open and one pool is overwritten
The second thread waits automatically because the constructor is private, so one pool is created
The second assignment throws an error, so one request fails and the other keeps the single pool
Two pools are created, but the unused one is freed at once, so no extra connections stay open
quiz.explanation: The check and the creation are separate steps, so two threads can both pass the check. The private constructor only restricts who may call it, not when. The losing pool is not cleaned up, so its connections can stay open until closed.

quiz.question: A TenantSettings singleton is read by 40 classes through getInstance(). Unit tests now leak state between each other, and the product team wants per-tenant settings next quarter. What is the best direction?
options: Keep getInstance() and add a map of tenants inside the singleton, still reached from everywhere
Make all the settings fields static, so tests can overwrite them directly
Pass the settings in through constructors, with a container creating one object now and one per tenant later
Add a reset() method on the singleton and call it in every test teardown
quiz.explanation: Injecting the dependency makes the one-instance rule a decision of the wiring code, so tests can pass a fake and the lifetime can change per tenant. A reset method or a global map keeps the hidden global that caused both problems. Static fields are even less replaceable.
